numberedLines.text: I am not in trouble. I want that said before anybody starts, because people keep walking
past this chair and doing the face at me.
The blue chair outside Mrs Farrell's office is a waiting chair. Farhan sat on it in
March because he handed in a wallet with forty pounds in it, and they gave him a pencil
with the school crest on and put his photograph up by the hatch. So.
What happens is, on Thursday I go past the Reception window at break and one of the
butterflies has already come out. It is hanging under the card with its wings going,
pumping them, which is the sign. You can look it up. If you leave them in the net after
that they get sad and start bashing themselves against the sides, and I am not going to
stand there and let that happen to a Reception butterfly while everybody else is playing
football.
Miss Deller did say nobody was to open the net except her. She said it on Monday,
though, and on Monday they were all still asleep in their chrysalises, so by Thursday
the instruction is basically out of date. I check with Marnie first. Marnie says don't,
Dilan. Marnie says don't about everything, including the water fountain last term, which
dried out in the end and was fine.
The net will not carry flat, so I put four of them in my lunchbox for the journey, with
the lid resting on top and not clicked down, obviously, because I am not stupid. Two
ride on my sleeve the whole way and do not even try to get off. I would say they chose
me. Nobody tells me the governors are in the hall.
It goes well, though. Mrs Kaur laughs. One of the governors holds his hand out flat and
a butterfly sits on it for about a minute while he stays completely still, and he says
something to the other one about a Painted Lady, so he knows what they are, which proves
they were ready. Miss Deller thanks me. She thanks me three separate times, quite
loudly, and then she sits down on the PE bench and has a long drink of water.
Reception are fine. Some of them are screaming, but that is just what Reception is like
at half past two.
There are twelve and we have got seven back, which is more than half, so as a percentage
it is a pass. Two are up on the beam over the stage where the ropes hang, and Mr Okafor
says nobody is going up there for a butterfly, not today. One is on the fire
extinguisher by the double doors and will not be moved. One went through the serving
hatch into the kitchen, which is not ideal. I would rather not say what I think about
the last one, because Mrs Farrell's office has a window in it that was open all
afternoon.
My lunchbox is in there on her desk. She is keeping it safe for me.
Mum is in there as well. She came at half past two, which is early for her, and she did
not say anything on the way past, she just did a small nod, which is our thing. I can
hear her voice through the door doing the short answers. I can hear Mrs Farrell say the
word "again", but that will be about the fountain, and the fountain was ages ago and
everybody has moved on from it.
Anyway. When they come out I am going to explain about the wings, because I do not think
Miss Deller had actually looked at them properly since Monday, and once you have seen
one doing it you cannot really leave it in a net.
The handle is going down. There is a butterfly sitting on top of the doorframe, right
above where Mrs Farrell's head is about to be, and I am the only person in this corridor
who can see it, and I am not going to be the one who tells her.
I stand up, because you stand up when somebody is about to thank you.
